description.narrative: Målet med insatsen är att individer, grupper i civilsamhället, kyrkor och institutioner bidrar till förbättrad social samexistens genom att på ett fredligt sätt lyfta bekymmer hos gruppen. Det huvudsakliga syftet med insatsen är: •Främjande av fredlig samexistens, ömsesidigt förtroende, och icke-våldsamma medel för konfliktlösning (detta inkluderar förändrade attityder mot varandra genom att jobba med historiska händelser och trauman, och att få färdigheter för att lösa konflikter fredligt). •Att främja fredliga sätt att uttrycka sitt missnöje på, och kräva sina rättigheter genom att uttrycka sina åsikter på ett konstruktivt vis.

The goal of the intervention is for individuals, CS groups, churches and institutions to contribute to improved social co-existence and to peacefully raising the social concerns of target groups. The main objectives of the intervention are: • Promoting peaceful co-existence and mutual trust, and promoting nonviolent means for Conflict Resolution (this includes changing the attitudes towards the other, dealing with historical grievances and trauma, and gaining the skills to resolve conflicts peacefully) • Promoting peaceful means for the communities to express their grievance and demand their rights through using their Voice constructively

sector.narrative: Civilian peace-building, conflict prevention and resolution

description.narrative:
The five target zones for the program are West Guji, West Arsi and Horo Guduru Wollega in Oromia region and Bench Sheko and Gedeo in SNNPR region. Communities in the program target areas have faced multiple difficulties. Children, women, elderly people and people with disabilities have been affected the worst by the ethnic-based violence there. The year 2021 has been very challenging, where two of the programme areas, Bench Sheko and Horo Guduru Wollega, are the sites of massacres leaving the communities traumatised. Three of the peace program target areas, Horo Guduru Wollega, West Guji and Bench Sheko, have been strongly affected by the ongoing conflict, while also disrupting the program activities in some of these target areas. Also communities in Guraferda, in the Bench Sheko Zone are suffering from hunger and lack of shelter because of the displacements caused by the conflicts.
Some of the major achievements during 2021 were as follows:
- Considering the contribution is smaller in its budget the impact of the intervention will not be at the larger scale. Therefore most of the achievements of this project can be seen in the behavioural changes of the target groups in the project area, that are traditional actors, religious figures, youth and women. This transformation of attitude from playing a role in igniting conflict to become an actor that plays an important role in creating lasting peace in the communities is an achievement by itself. As a result of this intervention many feels empowered to teach others about peace building and conflict resolution.
- Youth and women who took part in the peace building and trauma healing trainings have organised themselves voluntarily in networks to work for peace in Shashmene city and its surrounding. As a result these peace networks were actively involved in protecting and defending targets of the conflict from the mob attacks in Shashemene, following the death of the Oromo singer Hachalu.
- The peace trainings to the traditional leaders and religious actors from W. Guji and Gedeo communities have strengthened their capacities to play a crucial role in bringing these two communities, who were in conflict that led to the killing of many people and ended up in one of the country's largest internal displacement, to a dialogue by creating the linkage and becoming the bridge.
- This intervention has strengthened capacity of the Church leaders in the project areas and the church network has increasingly become a peace actor in the communities as they are now often called upon to the target areas to mediate when conflicts arise. Church leaders and young people are influential in the area of promoting peace and therefore strategic target groups for training on peace building.
- Women are taking up roles at the forefront of peace building efforts and not as a "parallel track" to a male-dominated peace mechanism. In the target areas, women, especially those with an already established position in their communities (such as the Hadha Sinqees...), are acting as peace agents. We see examples of women who took the peace trainings becoming peace ambassadors, leading their own training sessions on peace and increasingly becoming active in the peace building activities in their communities.
- The implementing partner (ECFE's networks) is increasingly participating in peace building activities in their communities. The task force that was formed as a result of this program is working on peace messaging both at kebelle and woreda levels. Also peace dialogues are being held between inter faith leaders, community elders and the local government officials, ensuring the strengthened collaborative efforts among the different stakeholders working towards peace.
Working with peace building activities in such a fragile and highly changing context as in Ethiopia is very challenging and it is understandable how results from such peace building programs needs longer period to be realised, as this deals with behavioural changes and social cohesion that involves a gradual process. Therefore, what is important for Sida to see in this peace program is how the process is going so far and if the bases and the seeds that gradually leads to a strengthened social cohesion and peaceful so-existence are being met through the intervention.
(EXTRACT FROM THE COMPLETION MEMO (Jan. 2024) PMU's result harvesting approach captured the added value of the project and enable to capitalize on learnt lessons for the next phase (contribution #16345). In a nutshell, PMU has met its planned outcomes consisting of: improved capacities of the evangelical churches to respond to peace needs in their communities and to address ethnocentrism in churches and society. women church leaders and women in communities are active in peace building, conflict resolution and trauma healing. evangelical churches strengthened to engage with stakeholders to advocate for peace in the communities. The project was implemented in West Guji, West Arsi and Horo Guduru Wollega in Oromia region and Bench Sheko and Gedeo in Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples region (SNNP region) during over 4 years (Nov. 2018March 2023) , including a first year for capacitybuilding and baseline surveys. The analysis of the baseline resulted to prioritizing the following aspect in the implementation of the project: 1. encouraging womens participation in the program, 2. increased sensitivity to other people, 3. the significance of the tailored peace model, and 4. incorporating indigenous knowledge of reconciliation. The project was challenges by COVID19 and the upsurge of the armed-conflict in Tigray, security constraint in Oromia challenging access and implementation of activities, but also the worse drought in 40 years and high inflation. PMU and its partner ECFE were agile enough to find ways to ensure the continuity of business. ECFE and PMU redefined the workplan several times. A no-cost extension request was granted, but despite this, ECFE could not absorb and use all resources and had to reimburse the balance of the contribution (0.7 MSEK, which is 10% of the grant) at the end of the partnership. Sida welcomes that the project generated a peacebuilding manual and a trauma recovery manual in the beginning that are still in use. It is satisfactory for Sida that ECFE and PMU report a transformation from violent means of expressions into nonviolent ones, and the program with its implementation strategy to mitigate outbreak of conflict and/or violence has empowered participants and promoted positive peace (Shalom). Churches capacity to address peace needs in their communities are improved, as well as their ability to address ethnocentrism in the churches and society. Churches engage in promoting stakeholders for peace, and women church leaders and women in the target communities are active in peace building, conflict resolution and trauma healing. Youth, women church leaders and male church leaders have all contributed to fostering peace and resolving trauma. It is positive as well for Sida that the project has reached its quantifiable outcomes, including the number of church leaders, women church leaders, and youth leaders who have received training in peacebuilding and trauma healing the growth of church engagement in peacebuilding and conflict resolution and, finally, the empowerment of evangelical churches to interact with other religions and pertinent stakeholders, such as the government. It is considered a positive sign by Sida that ownership and involvement, stakeholder engagement and existing structures provide all evidence for a sustainability of the program, and that in the absence of ECFE the programs sustainability is not questioned. Sida agrees with PMU that it is a good result in itself that peace messaging and intercommunity dialogue is taking place in conflict-affected areas where they are most needed. Church leaders trained in peace building are now often called upon in the target zones to mediate when conflicts arise, showing that the church network is becoming known as an actor for peace. Sida recognizes as well that ECFE has potential of being one of the best actors in solving the current and future peace uncertainties by minimizing durable conflicts and human violence in some part of the country. Sida appreciates that women were included in the project both as target beneficiaries but also as agents. It is satisfactory that the project contributed to the S/RES/1325 Security Council Resolution on women, peace and security, as women increasingly were empowered as peace agents in their respective communities. Sida recognizes the significance of women training others, both men and women: women are taking up roles at the forefront of peacebuilding efforts and not as a parallel track to a male-dominated peace mechanism. It is good to know as well for Sida that training on gender equality has in some places also included information about harmful traditional practices (HTP), and with the intention of eliminating HTP. Sida finds important that the project facilitated peace dialogues conducted for religious leaders, community elders, and government officials with the goal for them to learn about sustainable peace, to assess the individual contexts, and to develop action plans for peace. Importantly, it also gave the representatives of the different groups a chance to meet and discuss peace issues. Notably, the dialogues have gathered Muslim, Orthodox Christian, Catholic, and Evangelical faith leaders. The narrative report is ending with 5 impact stories highlighting the difference made by the project's specific outcome areas and for specific groups (youth, women, leaders, etc.)
